subject: Biology
title: Tool Use in Animals
description: A quick win: understand Tool Use in Animals.

hook.text: A New Caledonian crow bends a wire into a hook to fish food from a tube. No one taught it.

buildup.text: Tool use was once considered uniquely human. Then Jane Goodall saw chimps fishing for termites.

discovery.text: Dolphins carry sea sponges on their snouts to protect them while foraging on rough sea floors.

twist.text: Egyptian vultures throw rocks at ostrich eggs to crack them—a learned technique passed between generations.

climax.text: Tool use has been documented in mammals, birds, fish, and even octopuses.

quiz.question: What tool do dolphins use while foraging?
options: Sea sponges on their snouts for protection

details.summary: Tool use, once thought uniquely human, is documented in primates, birds, fish, insects, and octopuses. Chimpanzees use sticks to extract termites, crows bend wire into hooks, and dolphins carry sponges to protect their snouts while foraging on the seafloor.
details.whyItMatters: Tool use demonstrates cognitive flexibility and problem-solving across diverse lineages. Its independent evolution in species with very different brains suggests that complex cognition arises from ecological demands rather than brain architecture...
takeaways: Tool use has evolved independently in multiple unrelated animal lineages
Chimpanzee tool traditions vary between populations, indicating culture
New Caledonian crows manufacture tools with standardized designs

faq.question: What is the most sophisticated tool use in non-human animals?
faq.answer: New Caledonian crows manufacture stepped-pan tools from leaves with consistent designs passed culturally. They also combine multiple components to create compound tools, a level of manufacture previously attributed only to early human ancestors.

faq.question: Do any invertebrates use tools?
faq.answer: Yes. Veined octopuses carry coconut shell halves and assemble them into shelters. Some species of wasps use pebbles to tamp down burrow entrances. Archer fish spit precise water jets to knock insect prey off overhanging branches.
